key: Not our own will betrayed us, but seduction, thoughtlessness, Varuna wine, dice, or anger. The old is near to lead astray the younger: even sleep removeth not all evil-doing.
s: Told by the sages that Varuna is angry, the singer asks to be set free; Sāyaṇa, on 7.86.6, takes the cause of sin to be not a man’s own strength but fate fixed at birth, so the offence is one Varuna should forgive.

evidence.words: हे वरुण सः स्वोदक्षः पुरुषस्य स्वरूपवद्बलं पापपवृत्तौ कारणं न भवति किं तर्हि श्रुतिः स्थिरा उत्पत्तिसमय एव निर्मिता दैवगतिः कारणम् । … अतो ममापराधो दैवागत इति हे वरुण त्वया क्षन्तव्य इति भावः
evidence.gloss: O Varuṇa, that ‘own strength’, the power belonging to a man’s own nature, is not the cause of his turning to sin; what then? The fixed course of destiny (dhruti, printed here ‘śruti’), fashioned at the very time of birth, is the cause ... Therefore the sense is: my offence came by fate, and you, Varuṇa, should forgive it.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, 7.86.6 at [601,6]), two whole sentences, no dash. Sāyaṇa: sva dakṣa, a man’s natural power, is not the cause of sin; dhruti (printed śruti, glossed sthirā ... utpattisamaya eva nirmitā daivagatiḥ) is; and he closes that the offence came by fate (daivāgata) and Varuṇa should forgive it (tvayā kṣantavya). The sentence carries exactly this and omits his further gloss on the senior as God, so no drift. Wilson’s note on 6 and Griffith’s note on 6 report the same reading of Sāyaṇa. Plain sense faithful to 7.86.3 (the sages’ one answer that Varuna is angry) and 7.86.4 to 5 (the plea to be freed); no four-word run from the key. Revision 324074 dated 2021-11-09 by the wiki API. Entry-check ok.
